AccountResponse.description:
The caller's own account.

Overlaps ``CurrentUserResponse`` from ``/auth/me`` and is deliberately a
separate model. ``/auth/me`` answers "who am I, and what CSRF token should
I send" — it is part of the authentication handshake and carries the CSRF
token. This answers "what does my account look like", carries no token,
and is free to grow fields that the authentication path should not.

display_name.description: Null when the account has no separate label; render the username.
display_name.title: Display Name

last_login_at.description: ISO-8601, or null if this account has never signed in. On the caller's own account this is the *previous* sign-in's timestamp only until the current one records it, which happens at login — so it reflects the current session.
last_login_at.title: Last Login At

AccountResponse.title: AccountResponse

api_version.description: API major version served under this prefix.
api_version.title: Api Version

AuditActorResponse.description:
An account referenced by an event.

``username`` is null when the account no longer exists. The id is always
present, because that is what the trail actually recorded — see
:mod:`hcc.services.audit` on why names are joined rather than
snapshotted.

actor.description: Who performed it, or null for an operation with no authenticated actor.

details.description: Small structured context the writer constructed. Never credential material and never a request body.

target.description: Which account it acted on, or null where the action has no target.

Desired versus applied.

The distinction §23 insists on: a configuration the controller has saved is
not thereby active. ``status`` describes the gap.

CurrentUserResponse.description:
The authenticated identity.

Carries no password material and no session token. ``csrf_token`` is
included because the client needs it to make state-changing requests, and
it is useless without the session cookie.

One module's effective configuration on one host, with its provenance.

Both stored layers are reported alongside the resolved value, because
"inherited from the global default of 10 s" and "overridden on this host to
10 s" are identical in the value and are different facts.

host_override.description: The host's own override, or null when this host has none at all.

EnrollRequest.description:
What an agent tells the controller about itself while enrolling.

Every field is optional and advisory. There is deliberately no
``host_id``, no ``hostname`` and no ``host_name``: the host is decided by
the enrollment credential, and a field naming a host would be a field an
agent could use to claim a different one.

agent_version.description: The agent's own version string. Advisory, never trusted.
agent_version.title: Agent Version

EnrollRequest.title: EnrollRequest

EnrollResponse.description:
The agent's new identity.

``credential`` is the long-lived agent credential and this is the only
time it crosses the network in this direction. The agent writes it to a
file only it can read; the controller keeps only its digest.

credential.description: The long-lived agent credential, in plaintext. Store it with restrictive permissions; it is not retrievable again.
credential.title: Credential

heartbeat_interval_seconds.description: How often the controller expects a heartbeat once connected.
heartbeat_interval_seconds.title: Heartbeat Interval Seconds

host_id.description: The host this agent is now the agent for.
host_id.title: Host Id

host_name.description: Display name, so the agent's log and `status` output name the host an operator recognises rather than a UUID.
host_name.title: Host Name

protocol_version.description: The protocol version this controller speaks.
protocol_version.title: Protocol Version

superseded_previous.description: Whether this enrollment revoked a credential the host already had. True means another agent has just been cut off — reported so the agent's own log says it took over rather than joined.
superseded_previous.title: Superseded Previous

EnrollResponse.title: EnrollResponse

EnrollmentResponse.description:
A freshly issued enrollment credential.

**The only response in the API that contains a secret.** The credential is
not stored — only its digest is — so this body cannot be reproduced by any
later request, including a retry of this one. The interface has to show it
once and say so.

credential.description: The one-time enrollment credential, in plaintext. Shown once and never retrievable again. Single use, scoped to this host, and revocable until used.
credential.title: Credential

expires_in_seconds.description: Convenience for a countdown, computed server-side so the display does not depend on the browser's clock being right.
expires_in_seconds.title: Expires In Seconds

superseded.description: How many previously-pending credentials this issuance revoked. Non-zero means an earlier credential for this host has just stopped working, which an administrator needs to be told rather than discover by watching an agent fail.
superseded.title: Superseded

EnrollmentResponse.title: EnrollmentResponse

HostCreateRequest.description:
Register a host.

``extra="forbid"``: a request naming a field this model does not declare
is rejected. That is the mass-assignment guard at the boundary — a
forwarded ``lifecycle``, ``connection_epoch`` or ``id`` fails validation
rather than being silently dropped, and a client that believed it set one
finds out.

description.description: Optional note, up to 512 characters after normalization. Blank or whitespace-only is stored as null.

Consuming the new credential revokes the existing one and disconnects that agent, so the confirmation is the difference between a deliberate re-enrollment and a misclick that takes a working host offline.
allow_reenrollment.title: Allow Reenrollment

HostLifecycle.description:
How far through enrollment a host record has got.

A small closed set stored as a constrained ``varchar`` rather than a native
PostgreSQL enum. The reasoning is ADR-038's, applied here: this is not an
authorization surface, so a future member should not require
``ALTER TYPE`` — but it *is* closed today, so a CHECK does the enforcing.

HostResponse.description:
One host, as the interface sees it.

An allow-list. See the module docstring for what is deliberately absent

agent_version.description: As the agent reports it. Advisory and untrusted — it comes from a possibly-compromised host and is never used for a decision.

has_pending_enrollment.description: Whether an unused, unexpired enrollment credential exists. A boolean and nothing more: the credential itself is unrecoverable once issued.

HostUpdateRequest.description:
Change a host's labels.

Every field is optional, and "absent" is distinguished from "null":
omitting ``description`` leaves it alone, sending ``null`` clears it.
Pydantic cannot express that with a plain default, so
:meth:`to_service_update` consults ``model_fields_set`` — the set of keys
the client actually sent.

Labels only. ``lifecycle``, ``is_enabled`` and every connectivity column
are deliberately absent: enrollment state is changed by enrolling or
revoking, administrative state by the enable and disable endpoints, and
connectivity by an agent connecting. A field here that could set any of
them would let an administrator type a host into a state the system had
not reached.

description.description: Send a string to set it, null to clear it, or omit the key.
description.title: Description

environment.description: Send a string to set it, null to clear it, or omit the key.
environment.title: Environment

name.description: Omit to leave unchanged. Null is treated as omitted.
name.title: Name

HostUpdateRequest.title: HostUpdateRequest

LatestResponse.description:
A host's current values.

Empty when the host has produced nothing recent — not a list of zeroes.
The interface renders "no data", which is the honest answer and is
distinguishable from a measurement of zero.

One series a module produces, declared before any sample arrives.

The interface needs units and labels up front, so that an enabled module

Change the caller's own password.

Confirmation of the new password is deliberately **not** a field. It is a
client-side guard against a typo in a masked input, and the server has
nothing to compare it against that the client does not already have — so
sending it would mean transmitting the new password twice for no gain. The

No password material, and no token: the replacement session travels in

need to.

One point of a historical series.

``minimum`` and ``maximum`` are present only for a rolled-up tier. They

info.description:
Control plane API for Homelab Control Center — a self-hosted platform for
monitoring and managing Linux hosts, Docker containers and network devices.

This is pre-release software. The surface implemented today is identity and
access (authentication, sessions, users, audit), the host registry and its
enrolment flow, monitoring configuration, and metric ingestion and query.

Docker, logs, alerting, network checks and remote management are documented
in the repository but **not implemented**, and have no endpoints here.
info.title: Homelab Control Center

get.description:
Return the caller's account details.

Reads from the user already loaded with the session, so this costs no
additional query.

post.description:
Replace the caller's password, ending every session and issuing a new one.

Requires the current password even though the caller already holds a valid
session. A session proves possession of a cookie; changing a credential
should require possession of the credential, so that a stolen session
cannot be used to lock the real owner out of their own account.

A wrong current password is **422, never 401**. The client treats 401 as
"your session has ended" and signs the user out, so returning it here
would eject someone for a typo — see
:class:`~hcc.services.account.InvalidCurrentPasswordError`.

422.description: The current password did not verify, or the new one violates the policy. The two are distinguished by `error.code`.

429.description: Too many attempts for this account. Carries Retry-After.

get.description:
List every session that would currently authenticate the caller.

Only live ones. Expired and revoked rows are kept in the table so that
"when did this session end" stays answerable, but they are not what
"where am I signed in" means and listing them would bury the answer.

post.description:
End every session except this one.

Declared before the ``{session_id}`` route below so that ``revoke-others``
is not captured as a session id. FastAPI matches in declaration order, and
the parameter is typed as a UUID so the literal would in fact fall through
with a 422 rather than being mistaken for one — but relying on a
validation failure for correct routing is the kind of thing that breaks
the day someone widens the type.
post.summary: Sign out of every other session

post.description:
End one session.

Revoking the current session is allowed — that is a sign-out, and the
client learns on its next request, which answers 401. Refusing it would
mean one row in the list behaved differently from the others for no reason
the user could see.

A session id belonging to another account returns 404, identically to one
that does not exist, so this cannot be used to discover whose sessions are
live.

404.description: No live session of the caller's has that id.

post.summary: Revoke one of the caller's sessions

post.description:
Claim a host, once, with the credential an administrator issued.

The enrollment credential is spent by this call and cannot be used again —
including by a retry of this request. An agent whose network dropped
*after* the controller committed but before the response arrived has lost
its credential and must be issued another; that is the cost of single use,
and the alternative — a credential usable twice — is a credential that can
be replayed by whoever read it over somebody's shoulder.

**200, not 201.** Nothing addressable was created: the host already
existed, and what came back is a credential rather than a resource with a
URL. A 201 would imply a ``Location``, and there is none — there is no
endpoint that returns this credential again.

Every refusal is a 401 with one message. Expired, already used, revoked and
never-existed are indistinguishable to the caller on purpose; the audit
trail records which it was, because an administrator can act on that and an
attacker holding a stolen credential cannot.

401.description: No credential presented, or it is not usable.

post.summary: Exchange a one-time enrollment credential for an agent credential

get.description:
Return the action identifiers this server can record.

Served so the interface can offer a filter without hard-coding a list
that drifts from the server's. It describes what this build *writes*, not
what the table *contains* — a stored event from an older or newer version
may carry an action absent from here, which is exactly why the filter
accepts any string and the renderer tolerates an unknown one.

A constant, so there is no query and nothing to paginate.

post.description:
Verify credentials and issue a session.

Session fixation is impossible by construction: the token is generated
server-side from a CSPRNG and nothing the client sends influences it. Any
session already presented is revoked before the new one is issued, so a
token planted in the browser before login cannot survive it.

401.description: Invalid credentials. Identical for every cause.

post.description:
Revoke the current session server-side and clear its cookies.

Requires a valid session and a valid CSRF token: without the CSRF check, a
cross-site request could log a user out, which is a minor but real
nuisance attack.

Revocation is server-side and immediate. The cookie clearing is a
courtesy — the session is dead whether or not the client complies.

get.description:
Return the current user, and the CSRF token for subsequent requests.

This is how a client that has a session cookie but no in-memory state —
after a page reload, say — recovers both its identity and its CSRF token.

Return a page of hosts.

Available to every authenticated role, because a Viewer who cannot see the
fleet cannot use a monitoring product. Nothing in the response is
privileged: it is the same host metadata the dashboard renders, with no
credential material and no digests.

``limit`` is bounded by the query validation *and* clamped again in the
service. Two layers on purpose: this is the bound that stops an
authenticated caller asking the server to materialise every host, and a
bound enforced in only one place is one a future caller can route around.

post.description:
Register a host and return it.

The new host is ``registered``, enabled, and has **no** enrollment
credential. Registering a record and authorising an agent to claim it are
two decisions, and bundling them would mean every mistyped host also
minted a live secret with a fifteen-minute life.

409.description: The host name is already in use.

422.description: The name, description or environment is invalid.

get.description:
Return one host.

``host_id`` is typed as a UUID, so a malformed id is a 422 from the
framework and never reaches a query.

patch.description:
Change a host's labels.

Partial by design: a request naming only ``description`` leaves the name
alone. An empty body is accepted and changes nothing, which is the honest
answer — refusing it would mean the client had to decide whether its own
diff was empty, and a no-op is not an error.

Renaming is permitted, and the agent's access is unaffected: a credential
is bound to the host's id, not to its name. A host name is a label the
operator reads, which is why it is mutable where a username is not
(ADR-041).

409.description: The new name is already in use.

patch.summary: Change a host's name, description or environment

post.description:
Withdraw trust from this host's agent.

The agent is cut off at its next authentication attempt, which for a
connected agent is immediately: the controller closes a connection whose
credential has stopped being live.

The host moves to ``revoked``, which is deliberately not ``registered``.
The record has been used, and re-enrolling a host that once had an agent is
a different decision from enrolling one for the first time — collapsing the
two would hide the fact that a credential was ever issued.

A host with no live credential is a 409, not a success. "Revoked" and
"there was nothing to revoke" are different answers, and an interface that
conflated them would tell an operator their host is secured when nothing
happened.

409.description: The host has no active agent credential.

post.description:
Refuse this host's agent at the door, keeping its enrollment.

Takes effect immediately: a connected agent's connection is closed, and
further authentication attempts are refused while the host is disabled.

Distinct from revoking the credential. Disabling is "not right now" and is
undone by enabling; revoking is "that secret is no longer trusted" and is
undone only by re-enrolling the agent. An interface that offered one
control for both would force the operator to choose a consequence they had
not been told about.

Idempotent — disabling an already-disabled host succeeds and records
nothing.

Allow this host's agent to connect again.

Does not reconnect anything by itself, and must not: the controller never
dials out to a host (ADR-018). The agent is retrying on its own backoff
schedule and will succeed on its next attempt.

Mint the credential an agent uses to claim this host, once.

**The returned credential is the only copy.** Only its SHA-256 digest is
stored (ADR-042), so no later request can produce it — there is no "show
again", and the interface says so instead of offering a control that would
have to lie.

Issuing revokes any still-pending credential for this host, so the one on
screen is the only one that works. ``superseded`` reports how many stopped
working, because an administrator who issued a credential ten minutes ago
needs to know the old one is dead rather than find out when an agent fails.

A host that already has a live agent credential is refused unless
``allow_reenrollment`` is true: consuming this credential revokes that one
and disconnects the running agent, which is a consequence the caller has to
accept explicitly.

Issuing for a **disabled** host is permitted. Enrollment and connection are
separate steps, and preparing a host before enabling it is a reasonable
order of operations — the agent will enroll and then be refused at the door
until the host is enabled, which the host detail view states.

409.description: The host already has an enrolled agent.

post.description:
Kill an enrollment credential that has not been used yet.

The "I pasted that into the wrong window" action. Takes effect
immediately, and cannot be undone — issue a new credential instead.

Returns the count rather than asserting success, so "there was nothing
pending" is distinguishable from "one was revoked". An unknown id is a 404
rather than a cheerful zero, because a revocation that reports success
without having revoked anything is the one thing this must not do.
post.summary: Revoke a host's pending enrollment credentials

get.description:
The newest value of each series, if it is recent enough to be current.

The freshness window is the whole design of this endpoint. Returning a
host's newest sample regardless of age would let the interface present a
three-day-old CPU reading as the current one, and nothing in the response
would say otherwise. An absent series renders as "no data", which is
honest and distinguishable from a measurement of zero.

host is checked too: a series belonging to another host answers 404, the
same as one that does not exist. Told apart by nothing, deliberately — a
distinct error would confirm that the id is real.

get.description:
The question a chart cannot answer.

An empty chart could mean "nothing collected", "collection is off" or "the
agent is offline", and only the first is visible from the data. This
endpoint answers the first; the monitoring endpoint answers the second and
the host endpoint the third.

Every module in the registry appears, including those that have produced
nothing, so the interface can tell "this module has no data" from "this
module does not exist on this controller".

get.description:
Every module's resolved settings for one host, with provenance.

Reports the resolved value *and* both stored layers, because the question
an operator asks is not "what is the interval" but "why is it that".

delete.description:
Remove this host's override, so it inherits again.

A ``DELETE`` rather than a ``PUT`` of all-nulls: "stop overriding this
module entirely" is one intention and should be one request. Idempotent —
resetting a module that was already inherited succeeds, and is recorded,
because "did anyone try to change this?" is a question the audit trail
should be able to answer.

**200 with a body**, not 204. The caller needs the resulting revision and
sync status in order to show what the reset actually did, and a 204 would
make that a second request against state that may already have moved.

404.description: No such host, or no such module.

delete.summary: Make a host inherit the global default for one module

put.description:
Make this host differ from the global default for one module.

The response reports ``revision_created`` and the sync status rather than
just success, because §23 draws a line this endpoint sits exactly on: a
configuration the controller has saved is **not** thereby active. The
agent has to receive it, validate it and apply it, and until it does the
status is ``pending``.

404.description: No such host, or no such module.

422.description: The schedule was refused; every problem is listed.

put.summary: Set or clear one module's override on one host

get.description:
Every configuration this host has been given, newest first.

Offset pagination, unlike the audit log's keyset. The justification is the
scale: a host accumulates a revision per configuration change, which is
operator-paced rather than event-paced, so the deep-offset degradation
keyset pagination exists to avoid is not reachable here. The audit log,
which grows per request, genuinely needs keyset.

The documents themselves are not included — see
:class:`RevisionResponse`.

Return metadata about the running control plane.

Authenticated, not public. The release version and environment name are of
no use to a legitimate anonymous caller and of obvious use to someone
matching the deployment against known vulnerabilities.

What every host does unless it overrides it.

Every module in the catalogue appears, including those with nothing
configured — both fields null — so the interface renders the whole list
from one response and does not have to treat a missing key as a value.

put.description:
Change the fleet-wide default for one module.

**200, not 201.** Nothing addressable is created: the resource is the
module's default, which exists conceptually whether or not a row backs it,
and this endpoint is idempotent — sending the same body twice leaves the
same state and mints no second revision.

Regenerates the affected hosts' configuration revisions in the same
transaction, so a host's desired configuration cannot lag the default it
is supposed to inherit. Bounded: past
:data:`hcc.services.monitoring.MAX_EAGER_REGENERATION` hosts the remainder
pick the change up on their next connection, which regenerates anyway.

422.description: The schedule was refused; every problem is listed.

put.summary: Set or clear a global module default

get.description:
The closed catalogue, with the limits that bound every schedule.

Static for a given release — it is the registry, which is code — so it
takes no database session and does no query. Served from an authenticated
route rather than a public one anyway: the module list describes what this
deployment is capable of collecting, which is of no use to an anonymous
caller and of some use to someone profiling the deployment.
get.summary: Every monitoring module this controller supports

get.description:
Report whether an initial administrator exists.

Reads the installation row rather than counting users, matching the
invariant bootstrap itself enforces (ADR-033): an installation stays
initialized even if every account is later removed, so this must not start
reporting "setup required" when the last user is deleted.

``limit`` is bounded by the query validation *and* clamped again in the
service. Two layers on purpose: this is the bound that stops an
authenticated caller asking the server to materialise the whole table, and
a bound enforced in only one place is one a future caller can route
around.

The response carries **no password material** — not the plaintext that was
submitted, not the hash, not a token. An administrator who needs to give
the password to its owner already has it: they chose it.

422.description: The username, display name or password is invalid.

patch.description:
Apply an administrative change.

Partial by design: a request naming only ``role`` leaves the display name
and status alone. An empty body is accepted and changes nothing, which is
the honest answer — refusing it would mean the client had to decide
whether its own diff was empty, and a no-op is not an error.

409.description: The change would leave no active administrator.

post.description:
End an account's access.

Takes effect immediately: ``is_active`` is re-checked on every request, so
the account's next call fails whether or not its session has expired. Its
live sessions are also revoked, so the session counts an administrator
sees afterwards are accurate.

Idempotent — deactivating an already-inactive account succeeds and records
nothing.

409.description: This is the only active administrator.

post.description:
Restore an account's access.

Does **not** restore the sessions deactivation revoked, and must not: a
revoked token is revoked. The account signs in again, which is also the
only way the server learns the password is still known to its owner.

End every live session for an account, without changing its status.

Distinct from deactivation: the account may sign in again straight away.
This is the "I think that session was taken over" action, not the "this
person has left" action.

Returns the count, so the interface can report what happened rather than
asserting success. A revocation that reports success without having
revoked anything is the one thing this must not do, which is why an
unknown id is a 404 rather than a cheerful zero.
post.summary: Revoke all of a user's sessions

Public and intentionally uninformative. The version is available to an
authenticated caller at ``GET /api/v1/info``.

Verify every dependency required to serve traffic.

Public, so the response is an aggregate. Which dependency failed and why
goes to the log, not to an anonymous caller.
